newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian job rise welcome, but analysts cautious.
newsitem.headline: Australian job rise welcome, but analysts cautious.

text.p: Australia's stalled labour market showed signs of life in July, official data on Thursday showed, but analysts warned that it was too early to say that a recovery in employment was assured.
Total employment rose by 21,300 in July, close to median expectations of a 25,000 rise, but the number of people in full-time employment jumped a stronger than expected 52,500.
Despite the jobs rise, the unemployment rate moved higher, to 8.7 percent from 8.5 percent in June.
"I think we need a few more months of strong employment growth before we can shut the book on the weak labour market story," Toronto Dominion chief economist Gavin Stacey said.
The rise did little to change the view of a subdued jobs market which has yet to fully recover from May's 40,300 fall in employment.
Over the first seven months of 1997, total employment has risen by only 17,300 at an average of just 2,500 jobs per month.
But the most positive news for analysts was the big jump in full-time employment, one area of the labour market that has been particularly weak over the past year.
Stronger full time employment is seen leading to stronger consumer spending and economic growth.
However, despite the hefty rise, full-time employment levels are still below the level of July last year, and a total of 11,400 full-time jobs have been lost this year the data showed.
The government remains optimistic on the labour market.
While describing the current state of the market as flat, employment minister Amanda Vanstone said the outlook for jobs was positive heading into the end of 1997.
"The outlook for coming months is positive, however, with the effects of the most recent interest rate cuts yet to be felt," Vanstone said.

The stagnant labour market has been a key behind each of the five rate cuts delivered by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) since July 31 last year, and Thursday's data did little to change opinions about the likelihood of a sixth rate cut.

Those who believe the easing cycle has come to an end pointed to rise in full-time employment and said that given the 12 to 18 month lag between rate cuts and stronger growth, the conditions were in place for the labour market to improve.
"Our view is that we have probably seen the worst of the bad labour market news, with employment growth likely to pick up from here," Bankers Trust senior economist David Bassanese said.
Against this, those in favour of a rate cut pointed to the stubbornly high unemployment rate, and a stagnant labour market that has only created 17,300 jobs over the first seven months of 1997.

"Only one of the three volatile components of the labour force was strong," Westpac general manager of economics Bill Evans said of the full-time rise, pointing to a large fall in part-time employment and the higher unemployment rate.

When the first cut was delivered last year, the then RBA Governor, Bernie Fraser, noted that an earlier downtrend in the unemployment rate had stalled at around 8.5 percent. Since that first cut, the unemployment rate has not been below 8.5 percent.

"The unemployment rate is really stuck above 8.5 percent and we don't see that coming down in a hurry. The figures still maintain an easing bias to policy," Merrill Lynch Australia chief economist Nigel Douglas said.
